processing: Yunnan large-leaf tea is fired to stop oxidation, rolled and then dried in the sun; sun-drying is what separates it from oven-dried Dianlv.
harvest_season: Mostly spring for the better material, as is usual for Yunnan tea; lots are also made in other seasons.
appearance_dry: Long, coarse dark-green leaf with some silver tips, typical of sun-dried large-leaf maocha.
appearance_wet: Large, thick leaves, olive green when young.
taste_profile: Typically strong and brisk with bitterness that resolves into sweetness, and a sun-dried, faintly hay-like aroma.

brewing.notes: Typical settings for young sheng material. Slightly cooler water and quick steeps tame the bitterness.

vintage_note: Sold loose by harvest year and often by area, usually as fresh maocha, or pressed into pu-erh that is then sold by year. It can be drunk young or stored; storage is what moves it towards aged character.
description:
Dianqing is Yunnan's sun-dried green tea, made from large-leaf bushes. It is both a tea in its own right and the raw base for pu-erh, and the sun is the point: it is what sets it apart from oven-dried Yunnan green tea, Dianlv.

The steps are simple: the leaf is fired, rolled and laid out to dry. This sun-dried material, rather than oven-dried green tea, is what traditional pressed pu-erh is made from.

It tastes direct: strong, brisk and often bitter at first, with sweetness following. Use short steeps and don't take the bitterness as a flaw unless it lingers.

It is often sold as maocha under various names, and the terms overlap, so ask how it was dried. Oven-dried tea blended in is a common worry for pu-erh drinkers. Quality also varies by area.
history:
Sun-drying is described as the older way of handling tea in Yunnan, and oven-dried Dianlv took shape only in the middle and later twentieth century around the same large-leaf plants.

The term's exact boundaries are less tidy than they look. It is widely used for sun-dried large-leaf maocha, which is the base material of pu-erh makers such as Dayi, but no firm definition separating it from sun-dried maocha generally is well established.
